There is more to this than simply receiving and displaying small amounts of text. The server needs storage to handle the text, which is usually put into a database to allow features such as sorting, filtering and linking to other text records (e.g. comments). The database has certain overhead requirements to run optimally which are usually higher than some low end server can provide. The "code" needs some sort of web sever. That http server will need to handle many open sockets per second since even one user can open many sockets with one page visit. This is a bottleneck issue that can plague even large servers. The code itself must do many things. It must identify/authenticate the user, sort, filter and retrieve the data from the database, apply any rules/logic for how the page should be displayed, process any additional logic for maintenance of the backend data and finally put the HTML code together and send it to the user's browser. It must do this quickly or else users complain. While a single user request of one page may not put hurt on the server, have several hundred or thousands of these in a short time and the server will need a lot of resources to handle the requests in order to keep up with demand. Small severs will slow down or fail under these conditions.

Okay, sure there are improvements that can be made to optimize a site for small servers, but it's usually better to scale up a server and find the 80/20 rule where you spend 20 percent of your programming resources on gaining 80 percent of the efficiency needed. That last 20 percent will drain your programmers for very little gain. I think Voat is pretty much at the 80 percent mark on performance so more optimization would consume more programmer and server resources at a greater level. Scaling it to a distributed model can help, but that's a lot of work up front and in the long run. It also means more cost. 80/20 is hard to maintain.

The only way to accurately know what it might cost is to build it and give it a go. Initially your costs will be whatever amount you need to pay to just have a server and a connection to the net. Your costs will stay fixed for a while as your server can handle the load and your connection has enough bandwidth to support your traffic. Once your traffic increases beyond your bandwidth or the server's ability to keep up, your costs will then go up as you pay for more bandwidth or upgrade your server. It's a race between your popularity and your ability to self-fund your site since initially people aren't going to want to pay for using your site. Even later people will complain that if they give you money you will just spend it on yourself instead of the site (see Voat as an example) even though you're just trying to stop the constant bleed of money from your own wallet. All the while you now must spend you whole waking day responding to critics of how you put the whole site together, how you should improve it, how you should manage it and ultimately how you shouldn't do anything that looks like you sold out (see Voat as an example). Are you really ready to deal with that? Is it really about the cost of running a server? Are you ready to find out it's not just about a few kilobytes here and a few megabytes there?
